results.summary: This design implements a fixed zero-delay delay-and-sum beamformer that accepts up to 16 PDM digital microphones and produces an I2S audio output. It requires an external clock generator to supply a 3.072 MHz bit clock and 48 kHz LR clock, plus 16 digital microphones and an I2S receiver such as a Raspberry Pi. The documentation is largely placeholder text, so the internal signal processing and configuration details cannot be verified from the provided material. The pin names and external hardware list are the main evidence for its function.

This project implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game in Verilog with VGA video output and optional SNES-compatible gamepad input. Players move tiles using the ui_in buttons or a Gamepad Pmod, and the design includes a start animation, two color themes, and a unit test mode with debug pins. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. The design is notable for fitting a complete graphical game with input handling and debug support into a 2x2 tile area.

This is a simple Verilog ALU that uses a push button to switch between addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division operations. It expects switches for inputs and LEDs for outputs as external hardware. The documentation does not explain the pin mapping or how the operation selection works in detail, and the testing instructions are absent. It appears to be a basic educational arithmetic design with limited documentation.

This design is a 4x4 combinational multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product using layers of full adders. It is tested by placing inputs in a Python test script and comparing the output to the expected multiplication result. No external hardware is required. The documentation describes the structural approach and test method clearly, though it is a straightforward arithmetic block.

This project is a 4x4 structural array multiplier implemented in Verilog, with inputs q and m and output p. The documentation consists only of the title, pin names, and a note that no external hardware is needed, with no explanation of how it works or how to test it. The design is presumably a standard array multiplier based on the title and pin names. The lack of documentation makes it difficult to confirm any further details.

This design is a 4-bit array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit binary numbers using AND gates and full adders to produce an 8-bit product. It is tested by applying two 4-bit inputs and checking the 8-bit output against the expected product. No external hardware is required. The documentation explains the structural array approach and includes a diagram, making the design well described.

This project is a 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit numbers and produces an 8-bit product by computing partial products and summing them. It was tested with a test bench that applies various input pairs and checks the output against expected multiplication results. No external hardware is needed. The documentation describes the partial product method and testing approach, though the pin list only shows four output pins despite the 8-bit product description.

This is a 4-bit multiplier that accepts two unsigned 4-bit integers m and q and calculates their 8-bit product p. It is tested by providing several input pairs and verifying that the output equals the product of the two numbers. No external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand the basic function and test method.

DaDDS is an 8-bit direct digital synthesizer intended as an RF transmitter supporting OOK and FSK modulation. It accepts UART commands and frequency selection inputs, and outputs an 8-bit DAC signal. The documentation references architecture, UART protocol, and application diagrams but provides little textual explanation, so the exact operation and external hardware requirements are not fully described. It is notable for targeting high-frequency RF synthesis with digital modulation in a single tile.

This project implements a clock frequency sweeper that divides the input clock by 2 every 15 cycles, cycling from 1/2 to 1/16 of the input frequency, with an active-high enable input. It is tested in simulation with a test bench and cocotb, and on hardware by enabling the input and observing the output clock with an oscilloscope. No external hardware is needed. The design is a simple clock division experiment with clear documentation.
